# SK1001 — Use a collection expression

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A position whose type is already written out does not need the type written again in `new`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 12.0 |
| Since | 1.2 |
| Supersedes | IDE0028, IDE0300, IDE0301 |

## Why

`List<string> names = new List<string> { "a" };` says `List<string>` twice, and the second one is the compiler's job. A collection expression takes its meaning from the target type, which here is the type the author already wrote. The rule is deliberately narrow because collection expressions are the opposite of the usual modernization: they have no natural type, so `[…]` is legal in some positions and not in others, and an analyzer that fires everywhere fires where it does not compile. It fires in the three positions where the type is spelled by the author and the reader can see it — a declaration with an explicit type, a `return` in a member whose return type is written, and an assignment to a plain name — and only where the created object's type is that type exactly.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
string[] names = new string[] { "a", "b" };
List<int> ids = new List<int> { 1, 2 };
```

Write:

```csharp
string[] names = ["a", "b"];
List<int> ids = [1, 2];
```

## When it does not fire

None known. The proof is one comparison: a collection expression produces an object of its *target* type and the `new` produced an object of its own, so the rule fires only where Roslyn says the two are the same. That catches every widening at once — `object[] a = new string[] { … }` is an array of `string` that throws on an `int` write and `object[] a = […]` is an array of `object` that does not; `IList<T> x = new List<T> { … }` would let the compiler pick a different implementation. Beyond that it is silent on `var`, which has no natural type to infer and gives CS9176; on any type that is not an array or `List<T>`; where the creation has constructor arguments, since `new List<T>(capacity)` records an allocation decision the rewrite loses; on dictionary-style `{ k, v }` element pairs and on object initializers; on a lambda, whose return type is inferred rather than written; and inside an expression tree. ⚠ An argument is excluded even though the parameter type is written: `M(new string[] { … })` and `M([…])` need not resolve to the same overload, because a collection expression converts to several collection types at once. ⚠ One difference is real and accepted: `List<T> x = […]` may be built with an exact capacity where `new List<T> { … }` grows, so `x.Capacity` can differ. The elements, the type and the identity do not.
